That's everything needed. Here is the complete picture:

---

## Where to make the change

**File:** `httpx/_client.py`
**Method:** `headers` setter on `BaseClient` — lines **305–316**

```python
@headers.setter
def headers(self, headers: HeaderTypes) -> None:
    client_headers = Headers(
        {
            b"Accept": b"*/*",
            b"Accept-Encoding": ACCEPT_ENCODING.encode("ascii"),
            b"Connection": b"keep-alive",
            b"User-Agent": USER_AGENT.encode("ascii"),
        }
    )
    client_headers.update(headers)
    self._headers = client_headers
```

This setter is the **single place** where the client's default headers are assembled. Every outgoing request goes through `build_request` → `_merge_headers`, which starts from `self.headers` (i.e. `self._headers`), so anything added here is automatically included in every request.

---

## Minimal edit

Add your new header to the dictionary literal inside the setter:

```python
@headers.setter
def headers(self, headers: HeaderTypes) -> None:
    client_headers = Headers(
        {
            b"Accept": b"*/*",
            b"Accept-Encoding": ACCEPT_ENCODING.encode("ascii"),
            b"Connection": b"keep-alive",
            b"User-Agent": USER_AGENT.encode("ascii"),
            b"X-My-Header": b"my-value",   # ← add your header here
        }
    )
    client_headers.update(headers)
    self._headers = client_headers
```

---

## Why this is the right place

| Call chain | Role |
|---|---|
| `Client.get/post/…` | calls `build_request` |
| `build_request` | calls `_merge_headers(per_request_headers)` |
| `_merge_headers` | starts from `Headers(self.headers)` and overlays per-request headers |
| `headers` setter | **builds `self.headers`** from the hardcoded defaults dict + any headers passed to the constructor |

Because `_merge_headers` seeds itself from `self.headers`, any header you add to the defaults dict in the setter will be present on every outgoing request, and can still be overridden on a per-request basis (since `merged_headers.update(headers)` runs after).

---

## Where to make the change

**File:** `httpx/_client.py`
**Method:** `headers` setter on `BaseClient` — lines **305–316**

```python
@headers.setter
def headers(self, headers: HeaderTypes) -> None:
    client_headers = Headers(
        {
            b"Accept": b"*/*",
            b"Accept-Encoding": ACCEPT_ENCODING.encode("ascii"),
            b"Connection": b"keep-alive",
            b"User-Agent": USER_AGENT.encode("ascii"),
        }
    )
    client_headers.update(headers)
    self._headers = client_headers
```

This setter is the **single place** where the client's default headers are assembled. Every outgoing request goes through `build_request` → `_merge_headers`, which starts from `self.headers` (i.e. `self._headers`), so anything added here is automatically included in every request.

---

## Minimal edit

Add your new header to the dictionary literal inside the setter:

```python
@headers.setter
def headers(self, headers: HeaderTypes) -> None:
    client_headers = Headers(
        {
            b"Accept": b"*/*",
            b"Accept-Encoding": ACCEPT_ENCODING.encode("ascii"),
            b"Connection": b"keep-alive",
            b"User-Agent": USER_AGENT.encode("ascii"),
            b"X-My-Header": b"my-value",   # ← add your header here
        }
    )
    client_headers.update(headers)
    self._headers = client_headers
```

---

## Why this is the right place

| Call chain | Role |
|---|---|
| `Client.get/post/…` | calls `build_request` |
| `build_request` | calls `_merge_headers(per_request_headers)` |
| `_merge_headers` | starts from `Headers(self.headers)` and overlays per-request headers |
| `headers` setter | **builds `self.headers`** from the hardcoded defaults dict + any headers passed to the constructor |

Because `_merge_headers` seeds itself from `self.headers`, any header you add to the defaults dict in the setter will be present on every outgoing request, and can still be overridden on a per-request basis (since `merged_headers.update(headers)` runs after).
